extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent attorneys/agents, and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Examination-guidance for evaluating whether a patent application's specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1). Covers examiner methodology, standards for original and amended claims, biological deposits, inherency, incorporation by reference, and examples from case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description distinct from enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Ariad Pharm. v. Eli Lilly and Vas-Cath v. Mahurkar. Examiners should remember that proof of enablement does not necessarily satisfy written description (In re Curtis). The Guidelines are to assist in analyzing compliance with substantive law; rejections are based on law and are appealable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must convey possession to skilled artisan
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy the written description requirement, a patent specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Moba v. Diamond Automation, Vas-Cath. This is the central substantive standard; the inquiry is fact-based and depends on nature of the invention (Enzo Biochem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant shows possession of the claimed invention by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using such descriptive means as words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may also be shown by actual reduction to practice or by showing invention was 'ready for patenting' (drawings, structural or chemical formulas). Cite Lockwood; Pfaff; Amgen v. Chugai.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description is fact-based and varies with nature of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with the written description requirement is essentially a fact-based inquiry that will 'necessarily vary depending on the nature of the invention claimed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider predictability of the art and level of detail required; use case-by-case development (Enzo Biochem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claims presumed to have adequate written description, subject to examiner's prima facie showing
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; examiner has initial burden to present evidence or reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure describes the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Wertheim. Examiner may make a prima facie case by pointing out unsupported claim limitations and explaining why the disclosure does not show possession (Hyatt v. Dudas example).

rubrics_metrics.name: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description; the entire claim (preamble, transitional phrase, body) must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction is essential; consider preamble import, transitional phrase ('comprising','consisting essentially of','consisting of') and their effect on scope. Cite Katz, Morris, Genentech v. Chiron, Pac-Tec, Corning Glass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble and transitional phrase weighting in support analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The preamble language and transitional terms affect claim scope and the support required in the specification; 'comprising' is open-ended, 'consisting essentially of' is intermediate, and 'consisting of' is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant relies on a narrower meaning, applicant bears burden to show why; for prior-art purposes 'consisting essentially of' may be treated as 'comprising' absent clear specification language (PPG Industries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination limitations must be supported as a combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if individual elements are described, the specification must adequately describe the claimed particular combination of elements to show possession of that combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should explicitly point out lack of description of combination (Hyatt v. Dudas). Stored Value Solutions example (three authorization codes) shows each code may be described individually but not their combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: New or amended claims cannot introduce new matter; must be supported in original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: New or amended claim limitations that introduce elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violate the written description requirement (and the proscription against new matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support may be express, implicit, or inherent. Correction of obvious errors may be permissible if a person skilled in the art would recognize and correct the error (In re Oda). See MPEP §§ 2163.06–.07 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an essential or critical feature undermines possession
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that omits matter disclosed to be essential or critical to the invention as described in the specification may fail written description because the inventor did not convey possession of the broader claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Gentry Gallery, PIN/NIP, Tronzo v. Biomet. If specification describes a feature as 'the only possible location' or 'essential', omitting it can be fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional-only descriptions of biomolecule/genetic sequences are generally insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A biomolecule sequence described only by a functional characteristic, without any known or disclosed correlation between that function and the structure, normally is not a sufficient identifying characteristic for written description purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional descriptions that lack structural correlation (e.g., claiming sequence by function alone) typically fail; see In re Bell, In re Deuel and related discussion. See MPEP §2106 for subject matter eligibility guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description that does not render claimed invention obvious may still be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Under U.S. law, a description that does not render a claimed invention obvious cannot sufficiently describe the invention for written description purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Eli Lilly: mere disclosure that does not make the claimed invention apparent to skilled artisan may be inadequate even if it impacts obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposits of biological materials can help but do not substitute for written description
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposit of biological material may satisfy written description with respect to a claimed material, but a deposit is not a substitute for a written description of the claimed invention; the written description of the deposited material must be as complete as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Enzo Biochem; 37 CFR 1.801 et seq.; Final Rule discussion. Deposits made after filing generally cannot support additions or corrections to the filed disclosure; see MPEP and 37 CFR 1.804 conditions for corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency — inherent functions/theories/advantages disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: By disclosing a device that inherently performs a function or has a property, the application necessarily discloses that function, theory, or advantage even if nothing explicit concerning it is said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inherency requires extrinsic evidence showing the missing matter is necessarily present and recognized by persons of ordinary skill; probabilities/possibilities are insufficient (In re Reynolds; In re Robertson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference is treated as part of the application
rubrics_metrics.description: Information incorporated by reference into the specification is as much a part of the application as if the text were repeated in the application and should be treated as part of the filed text for written description purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacing incorporated material with actual text is not new matter. See 37 CFR 1.57(a) and MPEP §608.01(p); see MPEP §2181 for impact on 35 U.S.C. 112(f) issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner methodology — identify unsupported claim limitations and explain reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: After a thorough reading of the application, the examiner must point out the claim limitations that are not adequately supported and explain reasons why the claim is not fully supported by the disclosure to make a prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner need not present factual evidence but must make clear why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as describing the claimed invention (Hyatt v. Dudas). If examiner establishes prima facie, burden shifts to applicant to point to support or amend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's procedural burden when amending claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicant amends claims, applicant should point out where and how the originally filed disclosure supports the amendment; if applicant does so but disclosure still does not reasonably convey possession, examiner must explain why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite MPEP §§ 2163.04–2163.06 and Hyatt. A simple statement by examiner identifying unsupported limitation(s) may be sufficient in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laundry-list/genus disclosures do not necessarily describe every species
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'laundry list' disclosure of every possible moiety or a generic genus disclosure does not necessarily constitute a written description of every species in that genus because it may not reasonably lead skilled artisans to any particular species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Fujikawa and In re Ruschig. Demonstrating that skilled artisan would not immediately envisage the claimed product from the process disclosure undermines written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software disclosures: disclosure of functions can suffice where writing code is routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Where software constitutes part of the best mode, describing the functions of the software may satisfy written description because writing code for such software is within the skill of the art; flow charts or source code listings are not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Fonar Corp. v. General Electric: functional disclosure of software can be adequate in many cases; evaluate predictability and skill in the art.
